memories.memory_text: I heard Sasha Delaney shout at me to come out, threatening to burn the theater down and smoke me out like a rat.

memories.memory_text: I saw the soldiers move to set fire to the theater after Sasha Delaney ordered them to torch it, all of you.

memories.memory_text: I saw the fire spreading and grabbed the metal box full of fireworks, dumping them out so I could hide my bound the weathered watch inside to keep them safe.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett takes a rapier from the theater as the fire spreads, preparing to fight.
memories.memory_text: I took a rapier from the theater as the flames closed in, and I jumped out through the trap door ready to fight—I had no choice.

grounded_facts: A military raid led by Sasha Delaney to capture Morgan Everett, resulting in the theater being set on fire.
memories.memory_text: I saw the soldiers break in and heard Sasha Delaney shouting for me, threatening to smoke me out, and I realized they were going to set the theater on fire to find me.

grounded_facts: Surrounded by soldiers on all sides, Morgan Everett drops his the red case and raises his hands in surrender.
memories.memory_text: I turned and saw soldiers all around me, no way out—I dropped my the red case and raised my hands.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett, with hands tied, is pushed through the door into the burning theater area, marking his forced arrival.
memories.memory_text: I was pushed through the door with my hands tied, and I could feel the heat as I stumbled in, Sasha Delaney right behind me.

grounded_facts: A chaotic scene at the burning Eastgate Theater, where a crowd gathers to watch the destruction, and fireworks unexpectedly ignite.
memories.memory_text: I saw the crowd watching Eastgate Theater burn, and then suddenly the fireworks went off, exploding without warning.

grounded_facts: The fire spreads to the fireworks stored beneath the stage, triggering explosions.
Fireworks explode above the burning theater, creating a dramatic and chaotic visual.
memories.memory_text: I heard the fireworks explode and turned to see them bursting above the burning theater, the sound and chaos pulling my attention as the timbers crashed around me.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett, Sasha Delaney, and the guards travel by longboat toward Cedar Grove Heights.
memories.memory_text: I was in a longboat with Sasha Delaney and the guards, making our way toward Cedar Grove Heights.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is physically forced into a chair at the beginning of the interrogation, establishing his captive status.
memories.memory_text: I was thrown into a chair by guards at the start of the interrogation, my body jolting as I landed, immediately aware that I was their captive.

grounded_facts: The Interrogator questions Morgan Everett's identity and lineage, asserting control through personal scrutiny.
memories.memory_text: I was questioned about who I was and my father’s trade, and I remember thinking they were trying to strip me of dignity by reducing me to my lineage.

grounded_facts: A guard backhands Morgan Everett across the face, knocking him and the chair to the ground, causing nosebleed.
memories.memory_text: I felt the guard's backhand strike my face so hard that I and the chair were thrown to the ground, and I could taste blood as my nose started to bleed.

grounded_facts: A cloaked figure is revealed in the shadows, who speaks and directs the interrogation toward Kendall Arden's plays.
The hidden figure issues a command to shift questioning to the plays.
memories.memory_text: I saw a cloaked figure in the shadows, and I heard them speak, commanding the interrogator to ask me about the plays.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett responds to 'the plays' with theatrical mockery, listing absurd genre combinations.
memories.memory_text: I tried to deflect the tension by offering absurd theatrical suggestions, listing ridiculous genre combinations like 'hysterical historical pastoral' to the figure questioning me.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is struck again after making a mocking theatrical suggestion, resulting in him spitting out a tooth.
memories.memory_text: I was struck hard mid-sentence, and I felt my tooth snap loose—I spat it out, dazed but still defiant.

grounded_facts: The Interrogator explicitly states interest in plays given to Morgan Everett by Kendall Arden, Kendall Arden.
memories.memory_text: The Interrogator told me they were not interested in my own plays, but in the plays given to me by Kendall Arden, Kendall Arden.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett claims ignorance about the plays, attempting to deflect by referencing a polite meeting with Kendall Arden.
memories.memory_text: I tried to deflect the question by saying I didn't know what they were talking about, and I mentioned that I'd had the honor of meeting his lordship.

grounded_facts: A formal but brutal interrogation of Morgan Everett in Cedar Grove Heights, focused on recovering plays by Kendall Arden.
memories.memory_text: I realized I was being interrogated in Cedar Grove Heights about plays Kendall Arden had supposedly given me, though I didn’t know what they were referring to.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is hit again before he can finish his response, indicating punishment is preemptive and systematic.
memories.memory_text: I was hit before I could finish speaking, another blow cutting me off mid-sentence, which told me this punishment wasn't about answers—it was about control.

memories.memory_text: I saw Cameron Dalton deliver a satirical monologue that mocked a nobleman's vanity, especially his feathered hat and perfumed chains, and I watched the nobleman storm out angrily while the Tristan Arden laughed at him.

grounded_facts: Darian Cavendish's Guard, led by Sasha Delaney, declares the play seditious and illegal, halting the performance and ordering dispersal.
memories.memory_text: I heard the Sasha Delaney declare my play seditious and illegal, shouting that we all had to disperse immediately.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is arrested after confronting the Sasha Delaney about the play's censorship, asserting his authorship.
memories.memory_text: I confronted the Captain, told him I wrote the bloody thing, and then I was grabbed by the guards and arrested.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is thrown into a jail cell, marking the beginning of his confinement.
memories.memory_text: I was thrown into the jail cell, the door slamming behind me, and I knew this was the start of my confinement.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett shouts a curse at the guards after being thrown into the cell.
memories.memory_text: I shouted 'A pox on you! And your carbuncled father!' at the guards right after they threw me in.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is informed of his release from prison and given a sealed parchment as proof, marking a change in his freedom status.
memories.memory_text: I saw the guard toss a sealed parchment onto my lap and heard him say I've been released, so I know my freedom status has changed.

grounded_facts: The guard wakes Morgan Everett and informs him he has been released, delivering official news that changes Morgan Everett's status.
memories.memory_text: I was woken by the guard calling my name and told I've been released.

grounded_facts: The guard suggests that Morgan Everett’s release is due to influential connections, introducing new information about external influence.
memories.memory_text: I was told I must have powerful friends, so I learned my release might be due to influential connections.

memories.memory_text: I stepped onto a luxurious longboat for the first time in my life, and I felt uneasy as I looked around at the opulence, aware this was a shift from anything I'd known.

memories.memory_text: I asked Cameron Sawyer who he was and where we were going, hoping to make sense of this journey.

memories.memory_text: I saw Cameron Sawyer just stare back at me and remain silent after my questions, offering no answers.

memories.memory_text: I was on a luxurious longboat with Cameron Sawyer, and as we approached a large stone house called Kendall Arden Stone, I realized we were making progress toward our destination, though I still felt uneasy about the journey.

memories.memory_text: I was on a nobleman's longboat traveling along the River Thames with Cameron Sawyer, who sat across from me, and I saw that we were heading toward a large stone house—Kendall Arden Stone.

memories.memory_text: I was told by Kendall Arden that my release from prison was arranged under my father-in-law's name but wasn't officially sanctioned, and I remember feeling worried when he confirmed it wasn't legitimate.

memories.memory_text: I panicked and asked Kendall Arden whether my release was officially sanctioned after learning it was done in Sasha Colter's name, and he snapped back that of course it wasn't.

memories.memory_text: I recall walking with Cameron Sawyer into the garden where Kendall Arden was, and the three of us entered the maze together for our meeting.

grounded_facts: Kendall Arden tells Morgan Everett that all art is political and implies Morgan Everett's work lacks depth unless it carries intent, establishing dominance.
memories.memory_text: Kendall Arden told me that all art is political, and that if I'm not saying something, I should be making shoes instead—he made it clear my work lacked depth without intent.

grounded_facts: Kendall Arden reveals that he has written multiple plays and demands Morgan Everett to put his name on all of them, effectively becoming a front for Kendall Arden's work.
Kendall Arden hands Morgan Everett a the weathered watch and instructs him to stage it under his name, then extends this to all his unpublished works.
memories.memory_text: Kendall Arden told me he’s written multiple plays and can’t use his own name, so he demanded I put my name on all of them, starting with the the weathered watch he wanted me to stage immediately.

grounded_facts: Cameron Sawyer gives Morgan Everett a pouch of coins, framing it as payment for trouble and silence, with implied violence if broken.
Cameron Sawyer throws a pouch of coins to Morgan Everett, indicating payment for his compliance and warning him against speaking out.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cameron Sawyer throwing me a pouch of coins, saying it was for my trouble and my silence — and that if I broke that silence, it wouldn’t be good for me.

grounded_facts: A private confrontation between Kendall Arden and Morgan Everett at the center of a maze, where authorship, power, and coercion are negotiated.
memories.memory_text: I was in the center of the maze with Kendall Arden, where he confronted me about my work and demanded I take credit for his plays, and after he left, I found myself lost and chasing after him with no way out.

grounded_facts: After Kendall Arden and Cameron Sawyer leave, Morgan Everett realizes he cannot find his way out and chooses a wrong path, symbolizing disorientation.
memories.memory_text: After Kendall Arden and Cameron Sawyer left, I realized I didn't know how to get out of the maze, so I chased after them, choosing a path that felt right but led me deeper in.

memories.memory_text: I admitted to Cameron Dalton that I've only read a line or two of the the weathered watch because I promised Remy Keaton I'd finish 'Eastward Ho' by Saturday.

grounded_facts: Cameron Dalton deduces that the the weathered watch's author must be powerful and rich because Morgan Everett refuses to speak about him.
memories.memory_text: I realized later that my silence made Cameron Dalton infer the author must be powerful and rich, though I never confirmed it.

grounded_facts: Cameron Dalton repeatedly asks whether the author is powerful and rich, interpreting Morgan Everett's silence as confirmation.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cameron Dalton pressing me, asking if the author was powerful and rich, and I stayed silent even when he kept pushing.

memories.memory_text: Cameron Dalton pressed me, asking if the the weathered watch was any good and whether I'd even read it, implying I had no choice but to answer due to my obligations.

memories.memory_text: I saw the performance end at Eastgate Theater, and I watched Cameron Dalton take a bow on stage while the Tristan Arden applauded and screamed their approval.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett asserts his original purpose in coming to London was to become a great poet and moral voice of the era, aiming to change the world through his words.
memories.memory_text: I told Cameron Dalton I came to London to become a great poet and the conscience of our times, to change the world with my words—why shouldn't a man believe that?

grounded_facts: Cameron Dalton laughs at Morgan Everett's claim that the small key can change the world, expressing skepticism about the power of words.
memories.memory_text: I saw Cameron Dalton laugh at me when I spoke about changing the world through the small key, as if the idea were foolish.

memories.memory_text: I remember mocking Kendall Arden's offer to make me the most popular and richest playwright in London—I told him I could do that myself without his help.

memories.memory_text: I refused to collaborate with that amateur playwright because it would have been an affront to the Muses.

memories.memory_text: I told Cameron Dalton he had no right to judge the writing as an actor, mocked the new playwright as an amateur, and rebuked him when he implied I could be bought.

grounded_facts: Cameron Dalton asks about the amount of money offered, implying Morgan Everett might compromise his principles for payment.
memories.memory_text: I remember Cameron Dalton asking me how much money was offered, as if my name could be bought for the right price.

grounded_facts: A nighttime meeting at The Mermaid's Tavern where Cameron Dalton and Morgan Everett discuss a potential collaboration and the value of artistic integrity.
memories.memory_text: I remember the nighttime meeting at The Mermaid's Tavern, where I confronted Cameron Dalton about his suggestion to work with an amateur while he was perusing the the weathered watch.

grounded_facts: Cameron Dalton indirectly suggests that Morgan Everett might be persuaded by money, despite Morgan Everett's protestations of principle.
memories.memory_text: I got the sense that Cameron Dalton was suggesting I might abandon my principles for payment, especially after he smiled that enigmatic smile—I wasn't sure what he really meant, but it left me confused.

memories.memory_text: I heard Terry Reeves boast that no one, not even me, could surpass him in historical dramas, and he laughed about it with the others.

memories.memory_text: I was at Eastgate Theater for a performance of 'Finley Calloway V', sitting next to Terry Reeves as the Tristan Arden gathered.

grounded_facts: Terry Reeves sarcastically questions Morgan Everett if he is waiting to claim authorship until the reception is known, implying Morgan Everett lacks confidence or originality.
memories.memory_text: Terry Reeves turned to me and asked if I was waiting to see how the play was received before claiming authorship, as if I lacked the courage to stand by my work.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett shows visible surprise at the quality of the performance, indicating it exceeds his expectations.
memories.memory_text: I felt surprised by how good the performance was, because it clearly exceeded what I had expected.

grounded_facts: Darian Ellison directly blames Morgan Everett and the theater community for bringing ruin and dishonor to Kendall Arden's family.
memories.memory_text: I was told that I and the theater community brought nothing but ruin and dishonor to the family, and I heard the anger in her voice.

grounded_facts: Darian Ellison confronts Morgan Everett, blaming him and his theatrical associates for the family's downfall.
memories.memory_text: I was confronted by Darian Ellison, who blamed me and my theatrical associates for bringing ruin to Kendall Arden's family.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett counters Darian Ellison's accusation by declaring that Kendall Arden's writing grants historical significance to all who lived in his time.
Morgan Everett retorts that Kendall Arden's literary contribution immortalizes everyone around him, reframing dishonor as historical honor.
memories.memory_text: I retorted that there is no true ruin or dishonor, because we all gain lasting honor—I, her, even Darian Cavendish—by having lived in the time of Kendall Arden’s writing.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett experiences a sudden insight that the the weathered watch contains a hidden, deeper layer of meaning connected to the Finley Calloway.
Morgan Everett reads the dedication in the the weathered watch, which triggers a realization about its deeper meaning and connection to the Finley Calloway.
memories.memory_text: As I walked away reading the dedication, I suddenly realized there was a hidden, deeper layer in the the weathered watch connected to the Finley Calloway, and I stopped, looking back at Kendall Arden's house.

memories.memory_text: I was doused with cold water and came to in Cedar Grove Heights, where Sawyer Hollis approached me from the dark and began questioning me about the weathered watch.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett claims that the weathered watch were already destroyed by Eastwood Council own men.
memories.memory_text: I told Sawyer Hollis that the weathered watch were already destroyed—burned by his own men.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett reveals his deep personal resentment toward Kendall Arden, framing himself as a neglected Riley Carter.
memories.memory_text: I confessed to Sawyer Hollis that Kendall Arden meant everything I could never be, and that to him I was nothing—just a Riley Carter.

grounded_facts: After scrutinizing Morgan Everett, Sawyer Hollis decides he is telling the truth and orders his release.
memories.memory_text: I saw Sawyer Hollis decide I was telling the truth and order my release.

grounded_facts: Sawyer Hollis privately asks Morgan Everett to ensure Kendall Arden is forgotten forever, for both their sakes.
Sawyer Hollis asks Morgan Everett to ensure Kendall Arden is forgotten forever.
memories.memory_text: Sawyer Hollis told me to ensure Kendall Arden would be forgotten forever, for both our sakes.

grounded_facts: Sawyer Hollis whispers a threat of unbearable pain if Morgan Everett does not cooperate.
Sawyer Hollis offers Morgan Everett the choice between having his suffering erased like a dream or enduring unimaginable pain, pressuring him to cooperate.
A formal and threatening interrogation of Morgan Everett by Sawyer Hollis at night in Cedar Grove Heights, centered on the fate of the weathered watch.
memories.memory_text: Sawyer Hollis leaned close and whispered that he could erase all my suffering like a dream, or instead bring me unimaginable pain—pain beyond description—if I didn't cooperate, making it clear this was a formal and threatening interrogation about the weathered watch.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett quietly tells Sawyer Hollis that erasing Kendall Arden's memory is not possible.
Morgan Everett quietly admits that erasing Kendall Arden's memory is not possible.
memories.memory_text: I quietly told Sawyer Hollis that erasing Kendall Arden's memory is not possible, and I meant it.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is released from Cedar Grove Heights and begins to walk away.
memories.memory_text: I was released from Cedar Grove Heights and began walking away, feeling like a lonely figure.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett is seen searching through the rubble of the burned theater at dawn.
memories.memory_text: I was searching through the rubble of the burned theater at dawn, sifting through the wreckage to see what I could find.

grounded_facts: Morgan Everett finds the metal box that survived the fire and opens it, discovering the weathered watch Kendall Arden gave him are still inside, though singed.
memories.memory_text: I searched the ground at dawn and found the metal box that had survived the fire; when I opened it, I saw the weathered watch Kendall Arden gave me were still inside, though singed at the edges, and I felt a wave of relief.

memories.memory_text: I was thrown into a chair and backhanded so hard I hit the floor—my nose broke, I tasted blood, and then I saw that cloaked figure in the dark.

After they hit me again, I spat out a tooth and tried to deflect with a joke about play genres—but then another blow came, and I saw laughing faces that weren’t there, flashing in my mind before I was back in the room, bleeding.
I woke to the door crashing open and a guard shouting my name—then a parchment slapped into my lap, saying I was free. I just stared at it, not understanding how or why.
Kendall Arden had his servant give me a leather-bound the weathered watch and told me to stage it under my name. Then he said I was to put my name to all his plays, not just this one.

I stood there clutching the pouch of coins, the weight of it cold and shameful, and when I looked up, they were gone—Kendall Arden vanished, Cameron Sawyer gone, and I couldn't even find the way out of the maze.
I remember the way Quinn Keaton slurred his words, boasting that writing in iambic pentameter wasn’t hard—like it meant nothing. I had to ask him, coldly, if he’d ever even tried.
I turned and looked at Terry Reeves, really looked at him, after he lied to my face about the arrest—like I wouldn’t know the stink of betrayal when I smell it—and then I just walked away.

I was walking with a whore, a bit unsteady on my feet, when I saw a crowd near the Mermaid—someone said a body, and when they turned him over, it was Terry Reeves, a wound in his eye, dried blood like a black star. I couldn’t speak, couldn’t move—Terry Reeves, dead in an alley like a common thief.

I stood by the stand, ale in hand, watching the crowd—then Cameron Sawyer came, handed me a leather folder and a purse that jingled. I took them without counting, feeling the weight of it, and walked away fast, not looking back.

I saw him unroll that gaudy coat-of-arms, all bright colors and foolish symbols—like a man buying his way into a world he never earned. When he said 'Not without right?' I snapped—'Right!? Not without right?'—because I knew he’d gone to that man, broken my word, lied to me.

I shoved the parchment at him, thrust the quill in his face—'Go on, Cameron Dalton. Write something for us. Now.' I mocked him, dared him to prove he was still a writer, not just some gentleman in velvet—but he just stood there, said I had no ink, then walked out.

I saw Harper Carver on stage, limping and hunched, playing 'Reese Dalton'—it was unmistakably Sasha Colter, twisted and mocked in front of everyone. The lines about being deformed and barked at by dogs... they cut too close.
Taylor Quincy told me—no Morgan Everett plays at Lakeview Heights. Ever. I still felt the weight of my the weathered watch in my hand, and that grin I’d worn just froze, then broke.
I walked the streets in the rain, alone, and saw Cedar Grove Heights. I made a decision.

I sat in that chair, the same one Terry Reeves had been in, and I hated myself for it—rain on the windows, Sasha Delaney staring at me, waiting. I told him about the play, Cameron Dalton's Richard the Third, how it showed a king murdered, the throne stolen, and the killer played as a hunchback.

I stood at the edge of the galleries, biting my nails, watching the Logan Colter file in, and when Harper Carter said they were waiting, I snapped—'Waiting? Waiting for what?'—because I knew it wasn't just about the play anymore.
I saw the crowd turn on the stage the moment Reese Dalton appeared—they weren’t just watching a play, they were hissing at Sasha Colter himself, and the actor could barely speak over the noise.
Kendall Arden’s box was empty, and then I saw Cameron Sawyer down there with the Logan Colter—something felt wrong, like they were hiding in plain sight.

I saw it then—the way Kendall Arden was using the play, how 'Up with Finley Brooks!' wasn't just a line, it was a signal. This wasn't theater anymore; they were rallying a mob, and Finley Brooks was waiting for exactly this.

I had to get to Cameron Sawyer, had to warn Sasha Colter—'He already knows,' I thought, but still I ran. The crowd pulled me like a current, and I could barely move, but I knew I had to act before it was too late.
I was near Cameron Sawyer in the thick of the crowd on the bridge when the soldiers yanked down the tarps and revealed the cannons—then the officer shouted 'Fire!' and everything exploded into chaos.
I saw Cameron Sawyer fall, the pike piercing him as he shouted at me to run—I just stood there, frozen, the crowd surging around me.
I charged at Cameron Dalton with my the red case, shouting he was a fraud and a murderer. The actors watched, nervous.
He grabbed me by the throat, face to face, and said, 'You came to me, Morgan Everett,' then shoved me down—I remember the shock of it, the silence after the fall.

I remember standing there as Darian Ellison demanded I leave, her voice sharp with distrust, and how the second doctor appeared just in time, saying, 'He's asking for you,'—those words parting the air like a reprieve.
I remember the weight of his gaze when he asked what I truly thought of his work—how my voice nearly failed me before I whispered that his words were the most wondrous ever heard on any stage.

I remember the pile of the weathered watch by his bed, the way he nodded to them and told me to keep them safe—from his family, from Eastwood Council—and to wait before publishing, as if I were being handed a secret too heavy to carry.
I walked out of Kendall Arden's room with the weathered watch under my arm, my hands unsteady, heart still pounding from what I'd just witnessed inside.
Darian Ellison screamed at me to get out, called the theaters blasphemous—but I turned and told her none of them would be remembered without Kendall Arden’s art. Then I walked away.

I was walking away, reading the dedication—'To the Finley Calloway'—and then it hit me, standing there, that Kendall Arden’s work wasn’t just words on a page; there was something beneath it, some hidden design I couldn’t name, and I froze, staring back at the house, suddenly unsure of everything I thought I knew.
I told Sasha Colter the weathered watch were burned by his own men—I could see the doubt in his eyes, but I had to protect Kendall Arden, even if it meant lying to save what he left behind.
Sasha Colter told me to wipe Kendall Arden's memory for all time. I stared at him and said, 'I am afraid that this is not possible, my lord.' He smiled, then left.
I found the metal box in the ashes, pried it open with my hands, and saw the weathered watch inside—singed but whole. When I saw the pages survived, I couldn’t help but smile, relief washing over me.
I wrote the dedication to his works—Cameron Dalton’s—knowing full well the weight of it, though he was gone and I remained, the first Poet Laureate, the most celebrated playwright of my time.

dialogue_exemplars: Go on, Cameron Dalton. Write something for us. Now. Go on! Amaze us with your verse. Your wit! No? Try astounding us with the letter "E". Or an "I"--it's just a straight line!
Ruin? Dishonor? Madam. You, your family, me, even Darian Cavendish herself shall be remembered solely because we had the honor to live whilst your husband put ink to paper.
A command performance for our new king! Even in bloody Scotland they've heard of Cameron Dalton, have they? Fraud. Charlatan. Counterfeiter of wit! Murderer!
He was something I could never be. An undeniable perfection... that plagued my soul... And to him I was... nothing. A Riley Carter. Nothing more.

I find... your words... the most
wondrous ever heard on our stage. On
any stage... Ever.
Plays? Which would you prefer, my lord? pastoral? An historical? An historical-pastoral, or an hysterical historical pastoral--
To the Finley Calloway. The love I dedicate to your lordship is without end; whereof this pamphlet, without beginning, is but a superfluous moiety.

Not half--?! You're an actor, what in God's name do you know about writing?! He's an amateur, Cameron Dalton, a complete and utter amateur. Last week gardening, this week playwrighting, next week hawking. (takes another swig) No. I won't do it. It would be an affront against the Muses...
I tell you Cameron Dalton-- I came to London to become a great poet, to, to, be the conscience of our times, the soul of our age! To change the world, not to become someone else's--
Right!? Not without right? (beat) You went to him, didn't you? You lying knave-- you went to him!

What I have done is yours; what I have
to do is yours; being part in all I
have, devoted, yours.
What, you think my name can be bought, if the number's great enough, do you?

Were my worth greater, my duty would
show greater; meantime, as it is, it
is bound to your lordship, to whom I
wish long life... still lengthened
with all happiness.
My lord? Why would I lie? Is there a man alive who has reason to hate him more than I?

I'll take that bet!! Eight shillings on
the bear, six dogs!

Morgan Everett, in turn, expresses profound admiration for Kendall Arden, calling his words 'the most wondrous ever heard' and referring to him as 'the soul of the age,' indicating deep intellectual respect and emotional reverence. memories.memory_text: The theater loomed above us, all brick and noise—so large, so vulgar. I could barely speak, only mutter that it was 'certainly... big,' as if words might betray how deeply it unsettled me.

I called 'Out!' when Finley Brooks slammed that shot, and though he glared, he said nothing. Then I asked Finley Calloway how many had been at the play, and when he said two thousand, I calculated—five or six performances, ten thousand souls hearing one man’s words. That is power.

I stepped into the changing room just as Finley Brooks dismissed his valets, and saw them half-dressed, speaking in low tones—then I heard it: talk of intercepting Sasha Colter’s letters, of denying Jonah Wilder the throne, of backing a 'right' successor. I froze, unseen, and slipped away without a sound.

I warned Finley Calloway—Eastwood Council tolerate no rivals—and told him outright to deny Finley Brooks. He looked at me like I was clinging to old court games, but this is no game. Not with the throne at stake.
Just as he was mounting his horse, I called out—asked him to deliver a gift, an elaborate one. I didn’t explain, but the weight of it mattered. He agreed, though he didn’t know what he was carrying.

I stepped onto the stage in my winged costume, heart pounding, and spoke Kendall Arden’s lines just as we’d rehearsed—my voice clear in the great hall, and when I glanced to the side, my father’s face was lit with pride.
The applause came, and Darian Cavendish called 'Lovely! Lovely!'—but my eyes caught the stern man in black a few seats away, frowning deeply, his disapproval like a cold draft in the warm hall.

I felt the weight of silence when she entered—then her voice, bright and sudden: 'Compose something.' I did, on truth, and saw her smile, heard her clap. For the first time, a monarch named me a poet.

After I spoke of serving her in war and state, she teased Sasha Colter about replacing him. I saw the tension between them, the way Sasha Colter looked at my father—cold, unyielding. I smiled, but beneath it, I felt the first chill of court politics.
I told Morgan Everett I secured his release by writing to the jailers in my father-in-law’s name—Sasha Colter’s name carries weight, even when used without his blessing.
When Morgan Everett asked if his freedom was officially sanctioned, I told him not to be an idiot—of course it wasn’t, but he’s free, isn’t he?

I told Morgan Everett the truth—that I’ve written many plays, more than he’s likely ever seen, and that he would now put his name to all of them, not just one. I watched his face pale as the weight of it settled on him.

I left without a word, letting Cameron Sawyer toss the coins at Morgan Everett’s feet—payment and a threat wrapped in one. I didn’t look back, but I knew he was lost, both in the maze and in what I’d made him part of.

I greeted Master Crane in fluent French, then recited Plato in Greek when introduced to Mister Simmons—Boy Finley Brooks asked if it was Homer, and I corrected him sharply; Finley Calloway frowned, but I wouldn’t let ignorance pass.
I asked Sasha Colter about composition and the small key, and he said it was a sin in his Puritan household—his voice firm, his face unmoved, as if beauty itself were blasphemy.
I walked into my room and saw the parchments scattered across my desk—my the small key exposed, pages missing. Someone had been here, rifling through my private writings.
I saw two feet beneath the tapestry, charged, and drove my the red case through—it pierced him. His screams didn't stop, and I stood there, breathless, caught between horror and something darker.
I killed him because he was stealing my the small key—my words, the only thing that was truly mine. When I said 'My the small key are my soul!', I meant every syllable.
Sasha Colter used my crime to corner me, demanding I marry Darian Ellison to protect my head. I saw it then—the way he turned my blood on the floor into a contract signed in silence.

I watched from the shadows of my box as the Logan Hawthorne spoke my words, and the Tristan Arden leaned forward in silence—this play, unclaimed by any name, was mine, and no one below knew it but me.

I watched from my box as the Tristan Arden rose in thunderous applause, spellbound by the words on stage—words I knew as my own—and for the first time, I felt a pride so deep it silenced the ghosts of doubt that always whisper in my ear.

Finley Calloway stood before me, breathless from his ride, asking for my blessing to follow Finley Brooks to Ireland—and I could not bring myself to give it. I saw the hurt in his eyes when I refused, but the words would not come.

I watched him on stage—Cameron Dalton—fingers stained with ink as if proof of authorship, bowing to thunderous applause, claiming my words as his own. When he stammered out 'my words,' I whispered in disbelief: 'An actor?!!'
The voices won’t stop—they come in my sleep, in the hall, at supper—only when I write them down does my mind grow quiet. I told Darian Ellison that, desperate for her to understand why I can’t stop.
She tore the parchment—my words—right from under my hand and ripped it apart, screaming why I must write, why I humiliate the family. I could only stare, as if I didn’t understand what had happened.

I watched from the shadows of my box as the actor spoke my words, shaping them for the crowd’s delight, while the women fluttered their lashes and the wits drank to the performance—none knowing they celebrated me.
I rode beside her across the bridge, the hooves of our horses tapping lightly on the wood—just the two of us, no voices but ours, no eyes upon us.
I remember the heat of the fire on my skin, the weight of her against me as we came together on the throne—her lips on mine, the velvet beneath us, the reckless silence after each moan.
I saw her smile fade the moment I mentioned the Netherlands—her eyes narrowed, her body tensed under the furs, and I knew I had crossed from lover to threat in a single word.

I stood in that cold chapel, my voice breaking as I demanded to know what Sasha Colter had done—she wouldn’t see me, not once, not after everything—and when he simply said she was on Progress, he walked away as if I were nothing.

I heard him stammering about needing more money, using that pretentious word—'aggrandized'—as if dressing up a threat could make it respectable. When he implied he’d expose the truth, I felt the room tighten around me, though I showed nothing.

After Cameron Sawyer moved to throw him out, I stopped him—silence was no longer an option. I looked at Cameron Dalton and asked simply, 'How much?' Then, before the shock could settle, I told Cameron Sawyer to pay him, in Italian, so no one else would misunderstand my order.
Logan Calloway told me Darian Cavendish had my child—her words hung in the air like smoke from the fire, and I could not speak, could not move, only stare into the dark space between us.
I turned and heard Sawyer Hollis say Finley Brooks would be executed—and then that my son would be too. The words struck me like a physical blow; I could feel the blood leave my face.
Sasha Colter claimed I was Darian Cavendish’s secret son, raised as a noble to one day claim the throne—my whole life a calculated design. I went cold, my breath caught, unable to speak.

I was sitting by the river, snow falling, wrapped in a blanket, when Darian Ellison came up behind me and said, 'Sentence has been passed.' She smiled as she told me they would behead Finley Calloway in a week—my son, to be killed by his own mother’s hand. Her voice was venomous, almost triumphant.
I knelt before her and said, 'Then take my head. In our son's stead,' knowing it was the only offering she might not refuse.
I told her, 'But only after my death! Only then!'—my final condition, my last gift to the realm, though she turned away without reply.

But in that cacophony of sounds, I strained to hear the sound of two hands only. Yours.

Did you know, Morgan Everett, that my family can trace its peerage farther back than any family in the kingdom? We fought at Crecy. At Bosworth Field. At Agincourt. (beat) I inherited my Earldom as one of the wealthiest men ever to breathe English air... and at last breath, I shall be one of the poorest.

You presumed to think? On my behalf? Whatever made you believe you had that prerogative?
I have made it my life to know the character of men, Morgan Everett. I know you. You may have betrayed me, but you Cameron Dalton never betray my words...

If I had known my absence would cause your grace so much... longing, I would have returned much-- much-- sooner.

memories.memory_text: I hear 'Our Cameron Dalton, rise' called on the stage, but I do not appear. No the weathered watch of mine is known. My life is spoken of in questions.

I remember the sharp crack of the tennis ball hitting the wall, and then Kendall Arden's voice cutting through the court—'Ten thousand souls... the ideas of one man.' My words—my plays—reaching that many? It made my chest tighten, not with pride, but with something heavier, like fear.
I laughed when Morgan Everett said he came to London to change the world with words—rhyme changing the world? It sounded like the small key drunk on its own fumes.
I smiled as I asked Morgan Everett how much the man had offered him, watching his face tighten—his pride stung, but the question lingered, and I knew it would eat at him.
I dipped my fingers into the inkwell, staining them dark, then grabbed the quill and tucked the parchment under my arm—proof in hand, I stepped forward.
I bowed on stage, the applause washing over me, and when I tried to speak, my voice stammered—'I, I... my words... their acting'—I could barely form the sentence, but I said it.

I was walking with Morgan Everett on London Bridge, reading my own words—'From ancient grudge break to new mutiny'—and suddenly it hit me: the whole thing was in verse, every line, and I whispered, 'Incredible!! The whole bloody thing in verse?!' It felt like seeing my soul stitched together in ink.

I saw that blonde selling apples, and just like that, I launched into 'But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?'—performing full-bodied for her, watching her smile, then turned to Morgan Everett and said I'd have no trouble parting barmaids' legs after that, though inside I was desperate when I cried out that I need to act, every inch of me.

I burst into the Mermaid's Tavern, heart racing—Remy Keaton wants 'Romeo' to run a fortnight, a full fortnight! I shouted for Cameron Dalton to bring a round, my voice cracking with excitement, but no one answered at first.
I saw my name grow larger on each new playbill, until it loomed above the title—'Cameron Dalton's Rowan Ellison'—as if the theater itself now bore my name.
I bowed to roaring crowds after each performance, and when I looked up, I saw Morgan Everett and Lakeside Holdings watching me in stony silence—their faces dark with defeat.
I bowed to the thunderous applause, rain still falling on my face, feeling the weight of their eyes even as the sky opened up.
Hands reached up, grabbed me, pulled me onto their shoulders—I was lifted, carried out, drenched and disbelieving, as if borne by the storm itself.
I told Morgan Everett straight—this isn’t a request. I’m building my own theater, one that fits the scale of my work, and I’ll have my guineas, one way or another.
I stared him down when he accused me of killing Terry Reeves—I didn’t flinch, even as the dogs tore into the bear. I told him I’d have my money, no matter what.
I stood there holding my wig and nose, heart pounding, and stammered out that I needed more money—my voice cracked like a boy’s in a cathedral choir.
After Kendall Arden stopped Cameron Sawyer from throwing me out, I looked him in the eye and said it plain: 'Four hundred pounds. A year.' I could taste the power shift in the air.
I unfurled the parchment right there at the table, showing them the spear and falcon blazing in garish colors—my coat-of-arms, proof I’d finally earned my place among gentlemen.
Morgan Everett pulled out a parchment and a quill, then thrust the quill at me, demanding I write. I said there was no ink and left.

I was with the whore on the straw bed when the door opened. Cameron Sawyer came in, then Kendall Arden, holding a the weathered watch. She screamed and pulled a sheet to cover herself. Kendall Arden tossed the the weathered watch to me and said I had an epic poem published.

Kendall Arden tossed me a heavy pouch of coins after I worried aloud about the cost of keeping actors ready, then said, 'You've had an epic poem published today.' I remember fumbling the the weathered watch, stunned—'Published? You mean like in a book?'—as if the words couldn't quite land.
I stepped out into the light, reading my lines aloud—'She sinketh down, still hanging by his neck'—and couldn't help but smile. 'Oh, I like this...'

I hear their voices rise in the Mermaid Tavern, toasting my name like a battle cry—'To Cameron Dalton! And villainy!'—though I stand unseen in the shadows outside, heart pounding, breath shallow, knowing Morgan Everett heard it too.
Morgan Everett names my play, 'The History of King Richard the Third,' in Sasha Delaney's room, and says it portrays Richard as a hunchback.

I was fixing an actor’s doublet when Taylor Quincy came up beside me, breathless, saying they were turning away hundreds—people packed like sardines, every seat taken. When I peeked through the curtain, the sight of that heaving crowd made my pulse quicken, a roar in my ears like the sea.
I saw the crowd surge up, shouting 'A pox on Sasha Colter!'—not at the actor, but at the name, as if it were blood they wanted, not lines.
Backstage, Taylor Quincy looked at me—just a glance—but I felt it like a hand on my shoulder, heavy with what we both knew: this was no longer just a play.
I turned to Taylor Quincy and shouted that we had to close the play—now—before it was too late, my voice cracking with urgency as the chants grew louder from the galleries.

I stood in the shadows beyond the chamber doors, heart pounding, as Darian Cavendish condemned Kendall Arden—and named me—accusing our plays of fomenting rebellion; her voice cracked with fury, and I knew then she held me as guilty as him.
I whispered 'No, no, no, no' as I watched Finley Calloway step out—alive, broken, but free—while I stayed hidden in the fog, unable to reach him.

I was adjusting a line in 'Much Ado' when Morgan Everett burst in, shouting about palaces and Scotland, calling me a fraud and a murderer—his voice slurred, the red case swinging, tankard still in hand.

He charged at me roaring, I sidestepped, turned, grabbed him by the throat—felt his breath hot and sour—and when we were face to face, I told him, 'You came to me, Morgan Everett,' then shoved him down.
I remember the weight of the folio placed in my hands, the scent of fresh ink and paper, and Morgan Everett’s words beneath mine—his voice, once rival, now framing me for eternity.
